newsitem.title: USA: Indiana officials can't confirm latest CJD death.
newsitem.headline: Indiana officials can't confirm latest CJD death.

text.p: The Indiana Health Department said it could not confirm press reports that the death of a 62-year-old Indiana man was from Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), but said the state has several cases of CJD annually.
Jim Kosowski, director of public affairs for the department, said he was aware of the man's death from a newspaper report and did not yet have a death certificate to confirm the cause of death.
A wire service report on Wednesday said Joseph Gabor, 62, of Schererville, Indiana, died March 30 of CJD, a rare but deadly brain disease that eats holes in the brain, eventually killing the victim.
The disease has been called the human version of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), the "madcow" cattle disease that caused a consumer panic when detected in Europe in 1996.
The Indiana officials said CJD cases were "one-in-a million" in the United States and none had been tied to BSE.
"If that story is correct, an isolated case of this is not out of the ordinary," Kosowski said, adding that Indiana had nine cases of CJD in 1990, two cases in 1991 and three in 1992.
"The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) reports that they haven't found any cases of mad cow in the United States," said Jennifer Scroggins, an Indiana Health Department spokeswoman.

The wire service report linking Gabor's death to CJD sparked panic in U.S. cattle markets Wednesday. CME live cattle futures plunged the daily maximum of 1.50 cents per lb as traders sold the market down on ideas an outbreak in the U.S. could scare consumers away from eating beef.

In March, a U.S. Agriculture Department scientist said since 1990 department scientists examined brain samples from 5,427 high-risk cattle in 47 states and Puerto Rico through February 28, and none showed any sign of the deadly disease.

The U.S. government in 1989 banned cattle imports from Britain and two years later extended the ban to several other European countries. It also banned or restricted imports of animal feed, bull semen and fertilized eggs from cows in countries where BSE is known to exist.
In the wire service report, Gabor's wife said her husband may have contracted the disease from garden fertilizer containing bone meal that he spread on his roses.
